lesson.title: Accountability in practice: the record of processing
lesson.summary: Scale your measures to the risk, and keep a record of processing activities, including when small businesses must too.

prerequisites.reason: Every record entry states the purposes of processing.
Article 24 turns accountability into measures and policies.
The under-250 exemption does not apply to special categories.

blocks: Article 24(1) turns accountability into action. Taking into account the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing, and the **risks** of varying likelihood and severity, the controller must implement **appropriate technical and organisational measures**.
Those measures must ensure, and enable it to demonstrate, that processing complies with the GDPR. They must be reviewed and updated where necessary.
Where proportionate, the measures include **data protection policies** (Article 24(2)).
Following an approved code of conduct or certification can be used as one element to demonstrate compliance (Article 24(3)).
The key word is **appropriate**: a hospital and a bakery do not need the same measures.
The main tool for demonstrating compliance is the **record of processing activities** (Article 30(1)). The controller's record contains:

items: (a) the name and contact details of the controller, and of any joint controller, representative or data protection officer;
(c) the categories of data subjects and of personal data;
(d) the categories of recipients, including any outside the EU;
(e) transfers to countries outside the EU, where applicable;
(f) where possible, the time limits for erasure;
(g) where possible, a general description of the security measures.

blocks: Processors keep their own record of the processing they do for each controller (Article 30(2)).
Records must be in writing, which includes electronic form (Article 30(3)). They must be made available to the **supervisory authority on request** (Article 30(4)).
**The under-250 exemption** (Article 30(5)): an organisation with **fewer than 250 employees** does not have to keep the record, **unless** its processing:

items: is likely to result in a risk to people's rights and freedoms; or
includes special-category data or criminal-offence data.

blocks: Because any one of these defeats the exemption, it is narrower than it first looks.

Sunfield has about 40 staff, but it processes pre-orders and payroll every week, which is not occasional. It also handles sick notes, which are health data. So the exemption does not apply, and Sunfield keeps a record.

A sample entry: *Pre-orders. Purpose: fulfil orders. Data subjects: customers. Data: name, phone, order. Recipients: app hosting provider. Erasure: a set period after the last order. Security: access by role, encrypted backups.*

blocks.text: These Sunfield examples are **illustrations**. A real assessment depends on all the facts.

questions.prompt: How should a controller choose its data protection measures under Article 24?

options.blocks: By nature, scope, context, purposes and risk
options.reason: Article 24(1).

options.blocks: Identically for every business, whatever its size
options.reason: Article 24 requires appropriate measures, so they vary.

options.blocks: Only once a regulator demands them
options.reason: Article 24 applies from the start.

variants.prompt: Under Article 24, how are a controller's measures matched to its situation?

options.blocks: Identically for every business, whatever its size
options.reason: Article 24 requires appropriate measures, so they vary.

options.blocks: Only once a regulator demands them
options.reason: Article 24 applies from the start.

options.blocks: By nature, scope, context, purposes and risk
options.reason: Article 24(1).

questions.prompt: Which of these belongs in a controller's record of processing activities?

options.blocks: The name of every individual customer
options.reason: The record lists categories, not each person.

options.blocks: The administrator passwords
options.reason: Passwords are not record content. They must be kept secret.

options.blocks: The purposes of the processing
options.reason: Article 30(1)(b).

variants.prompt: What does Article 30(1) require the record to contain?

options.blocks: The administrator passwords
options.reason: Passwords are not record content. They must be kept secret.

options.blocks: The purposes of the processing
options.reason: Article 30(1)(b).

options.blocks: The name of every individual customer
options.reason: The record lists categories, not each person.

questions.prompt: Sunfield has 40 staff, processes orders every week and handles staff sick notes. Can it skip the record?

options.blocks: Yes, if it has never had a breach
options.reason: A clean history is not a condition in Article 30(5).

options.blocks: No, the processing is not occasional and includes health data
options.reason: Article 30(5): either condition defeats the exemption.

options.blocks: Yes, fewer than 250 staff is always exempt
options.reason: The exemption has three exceptions.

variants.prompt: Does the under-250 exemption help a small business that processes regularly and handles health data?

options.blocks: No, the processing is not occasional and includes health data
options.reason: Article 30(5): either condition defeats the exemption.

options.blocks: Yes, fewer than 250 staff is always exempt
options.reason: The exemption has three exceptions.

options.reason: A clean history is not a condition in Article 30(5).

questions.prompt: Who can require Sunfield to show its record of processing?

options.blocks: The supervisory authority
options.reason: Article 30(4).

options.blocks: Any customer who asks
options.reason: Customers have access rights, but Article 30(4) concerns the authority.

options.blocks: No one; the record is purely internal
options.reason: Article 30(4) requires availability to the authority.
